questions.q: Summarise the distributed-systems principles you apply as a Principal Engineer.
questions.a:
"I assume the network lies and design for it:

- Every remote call has a deadline; a timeout is an unknown outcome, resolved by idempotent retries, status queries and reconciliation.
- Exactly-once effects come from at-least-once delivery plus idempotency; events leave via an outbox; consumers keep an inbox.
- I choose consistency per data type: coordination for money and uniqueness, eventual consistency with explicit staleness for everything else.
- I avoid wall-clock ordering; I use versions, sequences, leases with fencing tokens.
- I contain failures with timeouts, bulkheads, breakers, load shedding and cells, and I test them with chaos and game days.
- I keep things undistributed until a measured force requires otherwise, and I make the safe patterns the default for every team."
pts: Deadlines everywhere; timeouts are unknown outcomes.
At-least-once + idempotency; outbox and inbox.
Consistency chosen per data type.
Versions, sequences and fencing instead of wall clocks.
Contain and test failures; distribute only when needed.

questions.q: Beyond leader-follower and quorum replication, explain chain replication, CRAQ and deterministic databases (Calvin). What problems do they solve and where do you see them in real systems?
questions.a:
### Chain replication
Replicas form a chain: **writes go to the head**, propagate node by node, and are acknowledged by the **tail**; **reads go to the tail**. Because the tail only has fully replicated writes, reads are strongly consistent without quorum reads.
- Strengths: simple strong consistency, high write throughput (each node forwards once), easy reasoning.
- Weaknesses: write latency grows with chain length; the tail is a read hotspot; a separate configuration manager (for example ZooKeeper-backed) must rebuild the chain on failures.
- Seen in: storage systems such as some object stores and block stores, and as a basis for later designs.

### CRAQ (Chain Replication with Apportioned Queries)
Lets **any node serve reads**: each node keeps clean and dirty versions. If a node's latest version is clean, it answers directly; if dirty, it asks the tail which version is committed. Read throughput scales with chain length while keeping strong consistency.

### Deterministic databases (Calvin)
Instead of running transactions and then agreeing on the result (two-phase commit across shards), a **sequencing layer** first agrees on a global **order of transaction inputs** (via consensus), and every replica executes them deterministically in that order. Replicas then reach the same state without per-transaction distributed commit.
- Strengths: no 2PC, high throughput for multi-partition transactions, replicas stay consistent by construction.
- Constraints: transactions must declare their read and write sets up front (or use a reconnaissance step); non-deterministic code is forbidden; long-running interactive transactions do not fit.
- Seen in: FaunaDB's design, influences on other distributed SQL systems.

### Why a principal should know these
They show the design space: you can buy consistency by structure (chains), by quorums, by consensus on outcomes, or by consensus on inputs. Choosing a database means knowing which one the vendor chose and what latency and failure behaviour follows.

### Core truths
Network is unreliable · timeout = unknown outcome · partial failure is normal · clocks lie · exactly-once effects = at-least-once + idempotency · some failures have no detector -> reconcile.

### Consistency
| Model | Use |
|---|---|
| Linearizable | Balances, uniqueness, locks (with fencing) |
| Causal / session | User sees own writes, ordered conversations |
| Eventual | Feeds, catalogues, analytics (state a staleness budget) |
CAP: during partitions choose refuse (CP) or accept-and-fix (AP) per data type. PACELC: otherwise latency vs consistency.

### Mechanisms
Replication (single-leader / multi-leader / leaderless N,R,W) · partitioning (hash/range/directory + virtual partitions) · consensus (Raft: majority votes + majority commit, 2f+1) · failure detection (heartbeats, phi accrual, SWIM gossip) · leases + fencing tokens · outbox/CDC · inbox · sagas with compensations · CRDTs for mergeable data · vector/Lamport/HLC clocks.

### Resilience
Deadlines propagated · retries at one layer, jitter, budgets · circuit breakers · bulkheads · load shedding · backpressure (bounded queues, 429/503) · hedging for tails (1 - 0.99^N) · cells · chaos tests and game days · beware metastable loops.

### Say this
"A timeout is an unknown outcome." "Consistency per data type." "Exactly-once is at-least-once plus idempotency." "Fence stale leaders." "Reconciliation catches what no detector sees."

### Added essentials
- **Write skew**: snapshot isolation lets two transactions write different rows from the same stale decision; fix with SERIALIZABLE, FOR UPDATE on the decision set, or a materialised conflict row.
- **Byzantine**: lying nodes need 3f + 1 and BFT protocols; enterprises use signatures, checksums, boundary validation and reconciliation instead.
- **TLA+**: model state, actions and invariants; the model checker explores every interleaving; use it for custom protocols where bugs lose money.
